My first duty is to congratulate the mover (Mr. Cayley) and seconder (Mr. Ferland) of the address upon their speeches last Friday. If I have any criticism to offer of the speech of the mover it is merely this, that with reference to the conditions generally prevailing in Canada he was rather too optimistic, taking all things into consideration. However, I take this opportunity of congratulating him upon his effort.
Now, we have had the privilege this afternoon of listening to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) as well as to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The prime minister has replied to the leader of the opposition, and I am not going to take up the time of the house to any great extent in criticizing the observations of either of these gentlemen. I think I have something to say of some importance to the people whom I represent and consequently I will not devote too much time to a criticism of these speeches.
One remark the leader of the opposition made struck me forcibly. While he admitted that we in Canada at the present time were enjoying an apparent prosperity, he warned the country to prepare for a possible deflation. I believe there is some truth in what the hon. gentleman has said, because we who are students of economics must know that while we have periods of prosperity, so called, these periods are always followed by periods of deflation; and it is my judgment that we in this house should take every step we possibly can to provide against the time of deflation when it comes, whether immediately or four, five or ten years hence.
One other remark I wish to criticize is the reference of 'the Prime Minister to the Crows-nest pass agreement. The western members know very well what this agreement means to western Canada. When we went into western Canada it was understood that we were to be protected by legislation in regard to grain rates. For war purposes this agreement was set aside for a certain period. The rates immediately went far beyond and above those specified as the maximum in that agreement.
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

Western members will recall particularly the year 1922 when the period of suspension of this legislation was about to expire. At that time there was a proposal in this house further to suspend the whole agreement for another term of years, and I am satisfied that had it not been for the stand which the western members took on that occasion the Crowsnest pass rates would not now be in force. I am willing to give credit to the government for everything which they finally did to make that rate agreement effective. The Prime Minister must remember that the committee which was organized to inquire into the question decided that this agreement should be suspended for a further term of years, and it was only after a review of the question again that the committee arrived at the conclusion that, as respects the Crowsnest rate agreement, the rates relating to grain should come into force on the 7th of July of that particular year. It was the western members who were primarily responsible for that agreement coming into force again. We remember also that in 1924, in order to make the agreement effective as regards grain rates, the government brought down legislation for which I will give them credit. They brought down legislation to make the rates effective on branch lines as well as on main lines, and for this the government must be given credit. At the same time, however, we must remind the government of this important fact: in order to pacify the railway companies or other interests, a part of the Crowsnest agreement was abrogated for all time; that is to say, on commodities originating east of Fort William the Crowsnest rate does not now apply at all. That is the situation to-day. "
Now I wish to take a little time to go through the speech from the throne and make a few remarks with regard to some of the items therein dealt with. I have not the time at my disposal to discuss every item, but I am going to deal with a few in which I am more particularly interested.
The first question to be considered is that of prosperity. I want to ask the government, where is the prosperity in Canada to-day? Are the working people prosperous? Are the farmers prosperous? I want to say that as far as my knowledge goes there is very little added prosperity among these particular classes, and after all they are the more important classes in this country. I am quite willing to admit that in certain quarters there is great prosperity, but as yet that has not reached the masses. Consequently it is futile for the Prime Minister and his colleagues to intimate to the people that we have great

prosperity among all classes in this country. I notice one very significant change in the way the part played by Providence in the production of our great crops is dealt with. I remember that in past speeches from the throne Providence was always given the credit for producing great crops in Canada, but now we find that the government has come to the conclusion that the farmers have some responsibility and deserve some credit for these great crops. This year we find the farmer sharing with Providence in the production of the great crops of this country, and with regard to the speech from the throne I think this is a very decided improvement.
Reference is made to the national research laboratories, and I commend the government for pushing to a conclusion this feature of last yeaifls legislation. However, there is one point which I would impress upon the Prime Minister and his colleagues; in conjunction with the research laboratories there should be a bureau of standards. To-day the Canadian people have very little knowledge of what they are buying, while in the United States the bureau of standards gives the people a proper intimation of the different* articles or commodities offered for sale from time to time. Under these circumstances the people of the United States are in a better positibn to judge as to the relative values of the goods offered for sale. I merely make that suggestion; no doubt it will take some time to get these research laboratories started, but I believe a bureau of standards should be created at the same time.
The speech from the throne also deals with the Hudson Bay railway, and calls attention to the fact that the railway is very close to Fort Churchill. I wish to take this opportunity of congratulating the government and particularly the Minister of Railways; since he has undertaken to create a port on Hudson Bay together with a railway leading to it, he has worked very hard. We all trust that when the Hudson Bay railway is completed and the facilities at Fort Churchill are sufficient to handle the business likely to go there, that port will be satisfactory in all respects as far as western Canada is concerned. I particularly congratulate the Minister of Railways for his efforts in that regard.
The next matter I wish to discuss is the question of immigration. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition dealt with this question, but I propose to bring before the house the viewpoint of the western farmer. I desire to read to the house the passage in question from the speech from the throne; the leader

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
of the opposition has done so already, but I wish to place a different interpretation upon it. It is as follows:
A flow of immigrants commensurate with Canadian requirements and selected strictly for their ability to promote the general prosperity of the country is being satisfactorily maintained.
I am going to turn my attention now to the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke). I remember that when he sat in our group he always maintained that more people were required in this country, and evidently he still holds to that point of view. But prior to his acceptance of his present high office his view might have been put in these words: "If you create conditions in Canada which will give the masses of the people an opportunity to make a good livelihood, you will have no need for an immigration policy. They will come here of their own accord." Indeed, I have heard him say that the great trouble would be to keep t'he people out. Does the minister still believe in that policy, and if so, what is he doing to bring it into effect? What efforts is he making in the councils of his colleagues to make conditions in Canada so good that people from all over the world will be rushing to this country and we will have great trouble keeping them out? Later on he will have the opportunity to give this house some idea of his efforts in that regard, but it seems to me that the present immigration policy is not satisfactory to anyone. I do not know of any person who is pleased with it, although I may say that since I have been a member of this house I have not known of a government policy, whatever the party in power, which was satisfactory to everyone. We must admit that the question of immigration is most difficult, and after all I think if we went back to the policy held by the Minister of Immigration before he accepted his present high position, we would be on safer ground than is the case at present.
I wonder very often whether the people of Canada, and particularly the members of this house, realize how quickly Canada has recovered from her post-war troubles. There is no question in my mind' that, considering the length of time we took part in the war, Canada has recovered from her post-war difficulties to a greater extent than almost any other country so engaged. In my judgment the reason for this is very obvious to any person who will give the matter a little consideration; the reason is that we have tremendous natural resources in relation to our population. Taking into consideration Canada's present population we have wonderful natural resources on which the attention
of ithe people has been focussed in the production of new wealth, and this to my mind has been the large factor in our remarkable recovery. In these circumstances we must realize that if we bring in a great volume of immigrants and the natural resources of the country become controlled by private individuals, it is quite reasonable for us to expect that we will not have even to the present extent the prosperity which would be ours with a smaller population. I am one of those who believe in letting this country grow naturally; I think the big trouble with Canada to-day is that people are always^ tinkering with it. If they would let it grow in its own way I believe everyone would be satisfied with the situation in a comparatively short time.
There is one point to which I wish to direct the attention of the Prime Minister ami his colleagues, and more particularly the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke). While it is quite true that British immigrants of all classes are permitted to come into this country, provided they can pay their fares and are mentally and physically fit, yet, in so far as the great bulk of the efforts of the department are concerned, there are three classes in which they are trying to secure new immigrants. These are domestic servants, farm labourers and agriculturists. Personally I am quite willing to compete against any farmer who cares to come to this country, but I do not want to be placed at a disadvantage in so far as that competition is concerned. I would like to see all other classes admitted to this country on the same terms as the agriculturalists. I do not see any reason why we farmers should be subject to the competition of new agriculturists coming into this country while the professions and even the working classes of Canada are being protected against such competition. We maintain that the time has come when this immigration question should be treated in the broadest way, and I take this opportunity of raising my protest against farmers being subjected to competition which other classes are not subject to.
Something has been said this afternoon with refeTenoe to the miners from Great Britain. The Prime Minister, in replying to the leader of the opposition, stated that the real reason why the government brought these miners in, or allowed them to come in, was that they might assist in harvesting operations in western Canada. I accept that statement as being the correct explanation of the situation. I would like to mention a little experience I had with a man who was working for me. This man came from Greau Britain some seven years ago. He came out

I am going to take the rest of my time to deal with a matter of vital importance to the farmers of western Canada, namely, the question of the Canada Grain Act.
The first statement I wish to make is that while the crop of last year is the largest ever grown in western Canada, it is my huimble judgment that that crop was not produced at a profit. I am' not going to say that it was produced at a loss, but the margin received by the farmer was so close to the cost of production that we can say that the crop was not produced at a profit. I think I can say that the crop was probably the greatest disappointment of any crop that has been grown in the west for many yeans past. This was due to climatic conditions, frost, hail and so forth, and consequently we cannot blame any one in that regard. The idea, however, seems to be prevalent, particularly in eastern Canada, that the farmers this year made a tremendous amount of money out of wheat. If you go into the small towns in western Canada the merchants there will tell you very quickly that the farmers at the present time have no purchasing power and consequently they could not have made a great deal of money out of wheat. Indeed, I am satisfied they did not make any money at all and if they broke even, they were lucky.
In a year like this it is only natural that the grading system should come under review and criticism by the person who produces the commodity. This year has been no exception to the rule. I have (heard more criticism
this year than I have ever heard before directed against the grading system and the farmer feels that the time has come when some better system should be evolved in regard to grading his wheat. The farmer maintains that the present system does not determine to any great extent the milling value of his product and it is on the basis of the milling value of his product that he receives a price for that commodity in the markets of the world. In view of the investigation of the agricultural committee last year into this question and the possibility of the matter arising again out of their report, I am not going to suggest any particular method or any particular change. I hope, however, that something may be done. The farmer of the west feels that just so long as the personal element enters into the question of grading his product, he will never have a satisfactory system, and I hope that ways and means will be found by the agricultural committee of bringing in a system that will be more satisfactory in determining the milling value of this particular commodity.

Mir. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was discussing the administration of the Grain Act by the Board of Grain Commissioners. As I have only another two or three minutes at my disposal I merely wish to make this concluding statement.
After reading the order in council passed by the government to bring the Grain Act into conformity with the amendment of 1927, I absolve the government of any responsibility for the "high power" tickets that were in use in western Canada last fall, and I place responsibility where responsibility belongs-on the Board of Grain Commissioners. Referring again to the special binned grain ticket, 1 would merely call the attention of the house once more to the part of the ticket which we believe the Board of Grain Commissioners are responsible for bringing into use:
Received into store from-[DOT]
Then follows a space for the insertion of the name of the farmer who delivers 'the grain. The "hybrid'' ticket which I have seen reads as follows:
Received into store on account of the Alberta Wheat Producers Limited.
We maintain that by virtue of such change being allowed the farmer was deprived: of the right of controlling the destination of his grain, and to that extent the change is a violation of the Canada Grain Act. We submit that the Board of Grain Commissioners are responsible for this violation, and therefore we ask that the present board be dismissed-no question about that-and that a new board be appointed. We suggest that the board be increased from three to five members, and1 that one of those members reside in Alberta and another in Saskatchewan. We recognize the influence of environment. Two of the present grain commissioners live at Fort William and the third at Winnipeg, and in their environment we believe that they are likely to be impressed by the grain trade to too large an extent. Consequently, for safety, we maintain that the board should be increased to five members, one of whom should reside in Alberta and another in Saskatchewan.
My time having elapsed, Mr. Speaker, I may be permitted to add that we farmers in western Canada hope that this house and the government will assist us in preserving our rights under the Canada Grain Act.

who on December 15 last spoke at a dinner given to the mayor of Montreal, who is also the member for Ste. Marie in the Quebec legislature. I am quoting from the Mqptreal Gazette of December 17, 1928, at page four:
Though the Conservative party suffered a disastrous defeat in 1896 from which it has not yet recovered, because of its efforts to maintain the spirit of the confederation pact in the matter of the schools of the province of Manitoba, yet the Conservative representatives from this province at the recent Conservative convention in Winnipeg, again secured the unanimous adoption of a resolution maintaining the traditional policy of their party in the matter of the schools of Alberta. For the benefit of argument, suppose for a moment we admit that the Conservative party is more friendly to French-Canadians than any other party. Now let us see what this martyr has to say about the way he has been treated by his own party. The hon. member continues:
Nevertheless there are tens of thousands-
Not only the member for St. Lawrence-St. George but several others.
-of English speaking Conservatives who have
voluntarily sacrificed all hope of personal political preferment

And I direct this to the attention of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett).
-by reason of their persistent efforts in defence of your traditions,-
That speech is addressed to French-Canadians.
-your rights, your privileges and your interests, of which the Conservative party in times past has been the chief support and stay.
Here is a strange contradiction. In the first part my hon. friend' says that the Conservative party is the party which is friendly to French-Canadians, and in the second part of his remarks he declares, "Well, we ourselves have had trouble with the same party because we have defended your rights". This is inconsistent. I Should not have believed my hon. friend had said it had it not been quoted

in a Tory paper. If it is true that the Conservative party is the party which is friendly to French-Canadians, how is it that so many Conservatives have suffered preferment because they have defended the rights of French-Canadians? If it is true that my hon. friend suffers now because he is supposed to have defended French-Canadians, how can his party be friendly to French-Canadians? That seems rather inconsistent and illogical in one of the brightest minds in this house. Let us continue-and here is a slur on all French-Canadian members from Quebec and even English members from that province who represent constituencies in this house. The hon. gentleman goes on:
What is the result to-day of the maintenance of the Liberal political bloc? Numerically, the Liberal representatives from the province of Quebec form the majority upon which the present government of Canada depends for a continuance of its political existence; yet, nevertheless, they are bound hand and foot to another, western, bloc, which actually exercises complete control, and whose economic theories and economic policies are subversive of your obvious material interests, and they the Liberal representatives of this province, are so obedient to the crack of their party whip that they always become dumb and speechless when issues, pregnant with dire import to you, to your province, to your ideals, to your traditions, are under discussion in the parliament of Canada.
I do not understand how one of our colleagues in this house can use such language in reference to sixty-one members from one province. I do not share the views of hon. gentlemen opposite; they have their own views and we have ours. But we respect each other. I do not believe we are all saints; no one of us is a saint, but we do our very best, and I believe my hon. friends opposite do the very best they can with a bad cause. I give them credit for their efforts. But no one has ever heard a member from Quebec say that all the members from Ontario or from any other province are not doing their duty in the House of Commons. Who ever heard such a statement? I find this very strange, and I could hardly have believed that this speech had been correctly reported had I not heard it myself on the radio. I was astounded to hear a respectable member of this house directing such remarks against sixty-one members who, while they do not share his political views, nevertheless hold him in respect.
May I quote one of the contemporaries of my hon. friend, the member for St. Lawrence-St. George-a man who, it is true, died some time ago. I refer, sir, to St. John Chrysostom, Bishop of Antioch, who lived in the fifth

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
century A.D. On one occasion St. John Chrysostom, quoting the scriptures, said: "The wounds of one who loves are better than the kisses of one who hates." The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George-I am sorry he is not in his place-kisses the province of Quebec, but he tries to wound the members of that province. Let me add, however, that like the old mortars the noise is great while the range is short. And perhaps the unsuccessful Tory -candidates in Quebec at the last general election owed all their troubles to the fact that they had, as an amulet for good luck, one hair of the Prophet's beard. I think this closes the incident.
May I now say a few words with reference to a matter of momentous importance. I refer to a question of principle which was brought up in the house last year and which I now bring forward again with the support of six of the nine premiers of the provinces of this Dominion-the question of public offices held by aliens. I have prepared a brief memorandum on the question. It reads:
In virtue of subsection 25 of section 91 of the British North America Act, aliens are under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament.
The first paragraph of section 123 of -the Cities and Towi^s* Act of Quebec (revised statutes of Quebec, 1925, chapter 102) enacts that aliens cannot be put in nomination for -nor elected to the office of mayor or councillor nor can they be a-ppoimted to any other municipal office. Article 227. paragraph first, of the Quebec Municipal Code is to -the same effect.
In 1926, in an act to incorporate the City of Arvida (16 Geo. V, Quebec, chap. 78, sec. 36) the legislature of Quebec enacted the following section:
''36. The following section is added for the city of Arvid-a, after section 123 of the Cities and Towns' Act:
. '123a. Notwithstanding the provisions of section 123, aliens may be appointed to and hold the office of -manager and the offices to be filled by appointment by the manager'."
During the last session, the legislature of Quebec passed an act to incorporate the town of Racine. Said act was assented to the 22nd of March, 1928. (18 Geo. V, Quebec, chap. 105).
Section 36 of said act is exactly the same as above mentioned section 36 of the City of Arvida Act.
By section 11 of 18 Geo. V. Quebec, chapter 105, Messrs K. B. Bolton and J. Reidy Smith are appointed aldermen of that city.
On May 25th ultimo, I was informed by the Department of the Secretary of State that those two people have never been naturalized, and in fact they are not.
This is the memorandum which sets the question before you, Mr. Speaker. I sent copies to the premiers of all the provinces, and the first reply came from Hon. E. N. Rhodes, Premier of Nova Scotia, who said:
Absence from my office in other portions of the province has prevented me from making earlier acknowledgment of your letter of June 26th.
The ground you take with respect to the holding of office by aliens is, in my opinion, undoubtedly sound.
That is the Rhodes scholarship in constitutional law that the Attorney-General of Quebec gets from Nova Scotia. Then I had a reply from the Premier of New Brunswick, who seems to be very friendly with the Premier of Quebec, since he has copied his liquor law. He evades the question, which is on public rights; there is no question of private rights. Any man in this country can hold private property and is entitled to the protection of our laws; a man from China or a man from the United States can hold private property here and be entitled to the full benefit of Canadian law. When it comes to public rights, however, it is entirely different; private rights may be vested in any individual, but public rights belong only to British citizens by birth or by naturalization, and when a man wishes to hold public office in this country he must comply first with our laws. That is most essential; our consti-ti-on contains this provision, and I am sure that statement cannot be contradicted. Here is what Hon. Mr. Baxter said:
With reference to your correspondence about the government of Quebec allowing Americans to be appointed to public positions without naturalization, I do not think I quite -agree with the legal interpretation in the memorandum -attached to your letter. The Dominion parliament, and that alone, can enact the conditions un-d-er which a foreign-born person may become a Canadian citizen. I do not think, however, that it is incompetent for a provincial legislature to provide that aliens may hold property of any description which the legislature may see fit. As a matter of fact, it was done years ago in New Brunswick.
The main track is my reference to Americans being appointed to public positions without being naturalized; the siding is in the words "I do not think, however, that it is incompetent for a provincial legislature to provide that aliens may hold property of any description," and the open switch is in the words, "it was done years ago in New Brunswick."

Let _ me now say in reply to the matter of your inquiry, that we have no Americans in our province and, consequently, we are not interested in the matter referred to in your letter.
This answer reminds me that Prince Edward Island is the province where they breed foxes.

I do not think it is any better for the French-Canadians to be Anglicized than it is for the English-speaking people to be Americanized. People should live according to their customs and their traditions, and individuality should not be lost in the melting-pot.
We have the greatest respect for the royal house here in Canada. In this country, as in every other British dominion, people prayed for the recovery of His Majesty the King. The King of England is a great symbol of authority. The royal family has occupied the throne of England for centuries. In the United States presidents come and go, while British royalty remains forever. I greatly admire the high ideals of the British people who put royalty above everything. They have great respect for His Majesty the King and all the members of the royal family. They are respected because they are human; they understand the needs of the people and they do their very 'best to help them. The prayers which were offered up for the speedy recovery of the stricken member of the royal family show that admirable reciprocity of feeling.
I have given to the house some very important documents and my friends on both sides of the house will be able to read them to-morrow in Hansard. I am sure that the Premier of Quebec will say in the Quebec papers to-morrow, "As soon as I have the full text of Mr. Pouliot's speech I will answer him." But the answer never comes because these facts are in conformity with truth.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: DEBATE ON MOTION FOR ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is very little in the speech that would indicate any very constructive program on the part of the government. It would seem almost as though the government, being fairly well entrenched, were going to repeat what occurred in the years 1921 to 1925, when the sessions were almost barren of real legislation. I would respectfully submit that anyone glancing over the notices of motion as put in by the private members will find a more constructive program than is contained in the speech itself.
We hear a great deal about the unprecedented prosperity of the country. I would suggest that much of this so-called prosperity is fictitious. We have had considerable gambling in stocks and shares, and although there has been prosperity in certain lines, for
instance in mining, the cream has been taken by a few individuals who control our great corporations. It is said that scores of millionaires have come into existence as a result of the rise in the stocks of simply three or four of these leading companies. As one, however, goes through the country, one fails to see any evidences of this much heralded wealth. In Saskatchewan, where I spent some weeks last summer, I was told in various districts that not since the pioneer days had 'land been as low as it is to-day. In Ontario it is very difficult to sell any farm that one imay wish to get rid of, and one has only to go down to the maritime provinces to find abandoned farms on every side.
When we come to our industrial life I would suggest that prosperity has not yet been made manifest in any larger wage being paid to the ordinary wage earner. There are no very recent figures with regard to this matter, but at the census of 1921 some very interesting figures were taken as to the distribution of our wealth. With respect to my own city of Winnipeg there is a table which shows the wage earners of ten years of age and over. This includes managers, bankers, brewers, doctors, clergymen, also some twelve judges and justices, these latter earning an average of $8,111 each. Altogether including these there are 46,223 male wage or salary earners and their earnings amount to $63,520,716, or an average of only $1,374 each. Any careful computation of the cost of living in this country will put the cost, in order to maintain a decent Canadian standard, at two-thirds as much more.
As regards labour, from 1917 to 1925, the figures for which are the latest available, the efficiency of production has increased 28.5 per cent, but in 1925 the number of employees relative to -the number in 1917 was only 87.5 per cent. Those are very striking figures- increased production but decrease in the number of employees. During that period the real wages advanced by only about 10.2 per cent and the prevailing percentage of wages to -total production was not much larger. The average wage in all the manufacturing establishments in -1925 was only $971. Again let me remind the house that according to evidence presented before a committee of the house it was said to take almost twice that much in order to maintain a Canadian family according -to what we regard as Canadian standards of living.
I would point out that employees of this government are receiving considerably less than $1,000 a year. If we are so prosperous and if we are able to reduce our debt at such
The Address-Mr. Woodsworth

a rate as our papers tell us is the case, it would seem that the least we can do is to see that our postal workers and others of that class receive a higher wage than they are receiving to-day.
But the trouble is not merely with the wages, but with the fact that there is such a large measure of unemployment. The departmental figures do not at all show the volume of unemployment, and as the superintendent oif employment service said, in evidenoe given under oath before the committee last year, during periods of depression a smaller percentage of the total number of unemployed was registered in our offices than in periods of prosperity when opportunities ' for securing work were greater. This simply means that when there is very little work to be had, the men refuse to go to the employment bureaux, and so the figures that are often quoted do not really mean very much. Let me give some idea of the situation by quoting a news item from the Winnipeg Free Press of January 9 of this year. Let me say that the superintendent of employment service verified these facts for me. This is the clipping:
"Some of them are suffering .actual hunger," said J. A. Bowman, this morning, superintendent for Manitoba of the Dominion employment service, in reference to a portion of the 600 unemployed men who haunt his office daily asking for work. The majority are single men and most of them are willing to take any kind of a job anywhere, he said, but no work is available.
That is true in most of our cities to-day. I turn to Vancouver, for example, and I find this warning issued by the city of Vancouver to the unemployed [DOT]
Unemployed Men Take Notice)
You are warned to keep away from the city of Vancouver this winter. No Work, No Doles. This corporation has laid down a plan to deal with the unemployed relief as follows:
(1) That absolutely no doles be given;
_ (2) That work such as breaking rock, clearing land, cutting wood, and moving dirt be provided for extreme eases of indigents only, after investigation, and as a relief measure, at two dollars per day for married men who are bona fide residents of the city, and one dollar in the form of meal and bed tickets per day for single men.
By order,
City of Vancouver.
That does not look like abounding prosperity for a very large and important class of our citizens, the transient workers, who have done an immense amount of the hard work of building our roads and cutting down our forests.

I come further east and recently the Montreal papers have been giving quite a bit of publicity to the health survey Which was made a short time ago. I give a summary of this from the Montreal Daily Star:
The survey revealed:
That the amount of money officially expended on public health in Montreal is lower than that of any of the twelve large cities with which comparison is made, being little more than one-half of that spent in New York city on a per capita basis and less than one-third of that of Pittsburgh.
That the infant mortality rate, although showing signs of betterment probably due to the improvement of the milk supply-is far greater than that of any of these twelve large cities, being more than twice that of New York and approximately 30 per cent higher than any other.
That the number of deaths from diarrhoea and enteritis in children of two years and under is the highest of any of the twelve large cities of the continent with which comparison is made, having a larger number of cases than New York with a population more than five times greater, and being more than twenty times higher than Rochester, nearly four times as high as Boston and nearly three times as high as Philadelphia and Detroit.
That the general death rate in Montreal is higher than that prevailing in any of the twelve large cities compared.
That the number of cases of diphtheria-a wholly preventable disease-was 1,854 last year, with 219 deaths, and that for the last fifteen years the number of diphtheria cases has never fallen below 1,000 and the number of deaths below 130.
That the inspection of school children is inadequate and inefficient and that educative work throughout the city, while showing an awakening in recent years, is still far below the standard of cities of similar size.
While it may be all very well for us to pass resolutions expressing our gratitude for the restoration to health of the King of England, it seems to me that this house has some responsibility for those thousands of preventable deaths in our own country.
Let me go still further east, if you like, and take another set of conditions that actually exist. A report was recently made by the City of Sydney Ministerial Association with regard to the long working hours and the wages paid in that great industrial plant in that city which has received a very high degree of protection and very great consideration from this parliament in times past. I quote a few paragraphs from the report of that committee:
For the continuous operations, consisting of the coke ovens, blast furnaces and open hearth departments, involving approximately one thousand men, the day term is eleven hours, and the night thirteen, throughout a seven-day week; that is, the men in these departments work an average of eighty-four hours every week-66 for the week on day duty and 102 for the week on night duty.

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
Again, the report says:
We believe that the plight-it can scarcely be called other-of the some one thousand men in the continuous operations is a scandal and a shame. To be on light duty, under the most favourable working conditions from eleven to thirteen hours were trying enough, but when we know the necessarily almost intolerable conditions in which these men have to work, heavy manual labour in gas, smoke, heat, and in some eases exposure to the elements, summer and winter, the situation is nothing less than appalling, and their treatment utterly abhorrent to the dictates of humanity. The only argument advanced by the management is the financial one-we are not in a position to give a general increase in wages nor the eight hour day.
Remember, this is in a time erf overwhelming prosperity. The report goes on:
Should the condition of the men with respect to wages and hours not be the first charge upon the profits of the industry?... Of the operating surplus $2,000,000 has been retained for depreciation.
And this query is put:
Should $2,000,000 of the profits of the industry, which the men at least had helped to make, be set aside, not for repairs, for these were taken care of in course of the operations and charged to them, but for future replacements, while not a cent o>f this amount has been allowed for the better condition of the human element in the industry? Unfortunately, it costs the industry little or nothing to replace men-there is nearly always a surplus of labour.
I do not think I need to add any further comment.
We are told in the speech from the throne:
A flow of immigrants commensurate with Canadian requirements and selected strictly for their ability to promote the general prosperity of the country is being satisfactorily maintained.
I shall not go outside the official statement of my own city of Winnipeg, in its report on unemployment relief for 1927-28. It seems that Last spring the Department of Immigration and Colonization registered the unemployed in Winnipeg. Out of 837 registered, 453 came to western Canada between December, 1925, and January, 1928, and of that 837, only 84 were Canadian bom. Although most of these immigrants came for farm work, 507 of them were unwilling to take up that work. Now I quote the report itself:
The spring unemployment situation brought to light the fact that country jobs are not being placed with the employment service of Canada, but that the Immigration department and the two large transportation companies and the land companies are obtaining them direct from the farmers through their very active work along this line as compared with no activity so far as the employment service is concerned.
The report proceeds-and I would ask the house to pay attention to this sentence: 78594-4
In consequence, in so far as country work^ is concerned, the man in the immigration office in Europe has a better chance of getting a job in western Canada than the mian in the employment office in Winnipeg.
That is a most serious state of affairs.
We have no mention whatever in the speech from the throne of what seems to be the most important problem before Canada to-day, and that is our relations with our great neighbour the United States of America. In recent years we have had two events at least of vast importance-the world war, which has reconstructed) what we used to know as "modern Europe," and released forces the effect of which cannot as yet be determined, and secondly, the rise of what might be termed the American United States Empire. Throughout a little more than a century the United States was united and consolidated and extended, and then during the past forty years it 'has become a great modem empire, changing the centre of gravity of the entire political world. Glance at some of the steps of this development.
Cuba, to all intents and purposes a protectorate. The Philippine Islands, under American tutelage, a strategic base for operations in Asia; China, the open door policy affording opportunity for economic penetration. The gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean sea, -almost an inland sea pf the United States, over which it exercises economic and political sovereignty, Panama and Central America, virtually under United1 States sovereignty. And then, through a sort of revised Monroe Doctrine, the United States is claiming hegemony over the western hemisphere with the exception, I may say, of Canada.
But what about Canada? Already the American investments in Canada are S3,313,-512,000, or 13 per cent of the estimated natural wealth of this country. If it were proposed that the border line between us and the United States should be moved a few degrees further north there would be a tremendous hubbub in this country, but the same patriots who would raise an army in such a case v'T -only look with equanimity upon the Americanization of this country, but further, they are glad to welcome any amount of this foreign capital for any purpose so long as they secure a certain proportion of the loot.
The United States, I say, is extending long arms to the north, and since the world war it has dictated the financial policy of Europe until, as a recent writer has put it, Germany is in danger of becoming an American colony. We have the Americans to-day sitting in Paris



The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
and dictating European policy. What is to be Canada's attitude to this 'increasingly powerful neighbour of ours?
First, let me say a word with regard to trade and the tariff, since that is the topic which we hear most frequently discussed when we are discussing our policy with regard to the United States. The indications, as we all know, point to the raising of the American tariff. Should Canada attempt to retaliate? That is a rather important question. I would say personally that it seems to me that Canada has in her hands a better card than that -the St. Lawrence waterway. The relation between this project and the American high protection policy were referred to in rather guarded language in the letter transmitted last year by our minister at Washington to the Secretary of State of the United States. I would think that so long as the Americans are anxious to build the St. Lawrence waterway, there is no particular reason why we should not be in a position to bargain very successfully to prevent the very substantial increase in the American tariff that is now threatened.
But with regard to the economic principle involved let me refer the house to a speech delivered by Sir Herbert Holt at the annual general meeting of the Royal Bank. He was dealing with the United States, but surely the economic principle which he enunciated ought to apply equally to Canada; so when he mentions Canada I have substituted the United States, and vice versa. Sir Herbert Holt's advice as an economist-I use his very words, but, "mutatis mutandis",-is:
-would seem that those who propose such tariff changes fail to realize that checks upon foreign (e.g. U.S.) prosperity automatically check the volume of goods which can be exported by Canada, and that on the other hand continued improvement in foreign conditions (e.g. U.S.) bring corresponding increases in the volume of goods which we can export. From this viewpoint it might be considered economic statesmanship for Canada to discover means to increase our exports (e.g. to U.S.) rather than to consider measures which will constitute new trade barriers.
. That, as I have said, is the principle enunciated by Sir Herbert Holt, but of course he applies it to the United States. By reference to the bank's annual statement it will bo seen that I have simply made the necessary changes to make the principle applicable to Canada.
In corroboration of this economic principle, so well stated, let me quote from the tariff manifesto issued in 1926 by a large group of European manufacturers and financiers. Unless I am greatly mistaken there was a 
reference to this very passage in the speech of Sir Herbert Holt. The manifesto contains the following:
There can be no recovery in Europe till politicians in all territories, old and new, realize that trade is not war, but a process of exchange, that in time of peace our neighbours are our customers, and that this prosperity is a condition of our own well-being. If we check their dealing, their power to pay their debts diminishes, and their power to purchase our goods is reduced. Restricted imports involve restricted exports, and no nation can afford to lose its export trade.
This is preeminently true of Canada, and I hope we shall not allow ourselves to be stampeded by the threatened upward revision of the United States tariff. You might as well tie a tourniquet around your arm to stop the flow of the arteries and then expect that the veins would not be at all affected.
Now let me speak of another phase of our relationship with the United States-what I might term international neighbourliness. I regret exceedingly that the speech from the throne gives no forecast of any legislation affecting the control of the liquor traffic between this country and the United States. Some of us several years ago supported the report of the special committee on customs and excise, and at that time we took it for granted that the government would loyally carry out the recommendations of that committee. What did that committee recommend? Let me quote section 10 of the report of June 18, 1926:
The committee further recommends that as soon os possible regulations be made to prohibit clearances being granted to vessels carrying liquor as cargo sailing from a Canadian port to a United States port, such regulations to make an exception in favour of liquor being imported into the United States in accordance with the laws of that country.
The report of the Royal Commission on Customs and Excise followed on October 15, 1927:
We also express our entire concurrence in the recommendation of the special committee of the House of Commons as contained in paragraph 10 of that committee's report. An effective method of carrying out the intent of the treaty referred to would be to prohibit clearances to vessels or vehicles of all kinds carrying a cargo of liquor to the United States contrary to the laws of that country.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is very poor policy indeed to do that which we know is a source of friction between us and the great and friendly country to the south of us.
But, further, our relationships with the United States are complicated by our relationships with Great Britain-another great im-

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
perial power. The Kellogg pact, which we are to have brought before us according to the speech from the throne, was stated by the Prime Minister to-day to be without American reservations. Well, I think he must admit that if there are no reservations, there is at least a very definite American interpretation. Mr. Kellogg said:
There is nothing in the American draft of an anti-war treaty which restricts or impairs
in any way the right of self-defence	
Every nation is free at all times, and regardless of the treaty provisions, to defend its territory from attack or invasion, and it alone is competent to decide whether circumstances require recourse to war in self-defence.
I may be permitted to give the very pertinent comment of Mr. H. N. Brailsford. He says:
But what is the use of outlawing war if each nation is left to decide for itself whether circumstances require recourse to war in selfdefence? Did any one ever hear of a nation declaring -war without insisting that its war was essentially a measure of self-defence?
And then undoubtedly there were British reservations. Sir Austen Chamberlain said:
There are certain regions of the world the welfare and integrity of which constitute a special and vital interest of our peace and safety. His Majesty's government have been at pains to make it clear in the past that interference with these regions cannot be suffered.
And so on. Mr. Brailsford again comments:
The extent to which, without the sin of "war" one may trespass on one's neighbour's territory, bombard his tovms, slaughter his citizens, blockade his coasts, and coerce his government to do that which it would not spontaneously do is one of the most surprising discoveries of our refined civilization.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put some questions which I hope the Prime Minister will take an early opportunity of answering:
1.	Why has Canada not renewed the Rush-Bagot agreement?-to which the Prime Minister referred in such laudatory terms in his speech at the ninth annual session of the assembly of the league.
2.	Why has Canada not intimated to Great Britain that she wishes to sign the optional clause of the Peace treaty? On July 28 last Premier Baldwin in the British house stated that there had been no intimation of this character from Canada. Why not?
3.	Why has Canada not adopted the genera! act for the pacific settlement of international disputes as drawn up by the ninth assembly of the League of Nations?-again an act which the Prime Minister, on the scene at the time, lauded in very high terms.
I would venture to suggest, Mr. Speaker, 78594-
that before having the Kellogg treaty brought directly before parliament we might very well have it referred to the committee on international relations which was set up several years ago. No question of international relations has ever yet been referred to that committee. Why not now set a precedent, and in that way allow the members of the house to become more fully informed concerning the details of this treaty, so that they may have a more definite voice in determining the foreign policy of Canada.
Now I come to another matter with regard to our relationship with the United States- the Anglo-French naval compromise. The Liberal amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne in the British parliament declared that the Franco-British naval compromise endangered the prospects of peace in Europe and of good relations with the United States. I take it that is not a jingo statement. And Mr. Lloyd George said that the Anglo-French pact was a complete reversal of the Locarno attitude. He is reported :
The treaty of Versailles and the covenant of the League of Nations contained undertakings by which the allies were bound to a general reduction and limitation of armament. Germany alone had fulfilled the undertaking. Where is the spirit of Locarno? Since Locarno the British, French and Italian armaments have increased.
Now I ask, was Canada consulted? You may say that this pact between Great Britain and France was not a treaty. No; but it definitely involved Canada. Was Canada consulted? Surely, if she was not, and if we are to be dragged into European complications through secret treaties, it is time we knew it. And if Canada was consulted I should like to know what advice Canada gave in the matter.
It seems to me that the least this house can expect is to have a very full statement from the Prime Minister at the earliest opportunity, as to what the situation is with regard to Canada and this discredited compromise. If the imperial conference declarations meant anything they surely meant that Canada has a right to express herself with regard to the foreign policy of the British Empire.
Had I time I should like to read a very interesting article on this point from Interdependence, the publication issued monthly by the League of Nations Society of Canada, in its November issue, in which this question is discussed in detail. Now it does strike me that the apparent policy of the Prime Minister and his government-Do nothing and sit tight-worked well in the Turco-Grecian affair. I had every sympathy with and com-

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
mendation for the position of the government at that time. That affair did not immediately affect Canada and therefore there was no difficulty. But this same policy might easily have meant disaster in this more recent ease, when American interests and hence ultimately Canadian interests were so vitally affected. Indeed, it seems to me that the Canadian government's policy at this time played directly into the hands of the big navy crowd in the United States. Again I ask, was Canada consulted? And, if so, what advice did Canada give, and why did Canada not rise to the occasion and prevent the fiasco which occurred and which had to be condemned by the Liberal party in the present session of the British parliament?
I wish to speak for a moment of the menace of Anglo-American naval rivalry. I will not quote here what possibly might quite rightly be termed the jingo speeches of Coolidge, or Birkenhead, or the Dean of St. Paul's. I will quote, however, a statement by Norman Angell, who says:
We get, therefore, immediately following the solemn outlawry of war, a nearer approach the old alliance and balance of power situation than Europe has known since the armistice; a worsening of Anglo-American relations and what would seem to be the beginning of an Anglo-American naval rivalry to follow the Anglo-German of a quarter of a century ago; a worsening of Anglo-German relations; an all but complete breakdown of the effort to secure even a conference about disarmament.
Or let us take the Manchester Guardian, which is not a jingo paper. That organ speaks of:
-ill feeling, suspicion, misunderstanding estrangement between the two nationsand affirms that:
and
,, no*, many years have the Americans and the British been on terms as bad as they are now.
Mr. Fred A Britten of Illinois, chairman of the house committee on naval affairs, who made a well-intentioned if perhaps rather improper move a little while ago in his effort to secure better relations, recently said:
America's desire for the free use of the seas cannot be assured by paper agreements alone. Steel ships with big guns accompanied by airplanes speak with much greater force than timeworn words of friendly treaties.
I submit that the hush policy is no good. I think Ramsay MacDonald gave a lead in courageously facing the actual facts in the world situation to-day. What is the real difficulty? Personally, I would say I am one of those who believe that fundamentally the trouble is that there are conflicting economic
fM.r. Woodsworth.]
interests between these two great imperial powers. That I will not now discuss. But so far as the political and diplomatic side is concerned, the trouble seems to be due to differing conceptions of the freedom of the seas. I would call attention to the very carefully stated position of the New York World:
Beneath all the wild talk on both sides of the Atlantic there is this cardinal fact, which is the root of the whole controversy. The British Admiralty, and that part of the British nation which shares its views, holds fast to the claim that Great Britain shall have the power to say who shall and who shall not sail the sea in ships. It is a claim which would put the interest of all other powers in jeopardy whenever Great Britain is at war. It is an impossible claim, looked at from any non-British point of view, for it amounts to saying that the interest of mankind upon the seas shall in law and in fact be subject to the will of the British Admiralty. It is resistance to this claim which explains the whole controversy.
And from the British side, in his recent work, "Freedom of the Seas'', Commander Kenworthy says:
The British will have to envisage now the eventual renunciation of the right of independent blockade instead of, as now, tacitly recognizing that in future it will be impossible to enforce it without American approval; while the Americans will have to envisage now, eventually recognizing, that freedom of the seas and sea law cannot be guaranteed without an Anglo-American convention which will have to be brought into relation with the covenant of the league.
I ask again, what is Canada's position with regard to this very important question, the freedom of the seas? We ought to have some definite policy in the matter. In case of war between Great Britain and the United States what would happen? We hate to contemplate such a contingency. We say the thing is impossible; and yet men, both in the United States and in Great Britain, are speculating with reference to this and in both countries the building of huge navies is inexplicable unless, in the background of the minds of some at least, there is an idea that conflict is possible.
And what about Canada in the event of such a war? I should like to quote an editorial which recently appeared in the Western Producer, a paper which has a wide influence in the west and whose editor cannot be called either unpatriotic or pusillanimous. He discusses this matter at some length -I am afraid I have not time to read the whole editorial-observing in conclusion:
There is only one way for Canada to retain her independence and her self-respect and that is by being decent and unprovoking. Canada

The Address-Mr. Adshead
cannot possibly engage in hostilities with the United States, on her own account, or in alliance with any possible combination, British or otherwise, without encountering complete disaster. It might be just as well to realize this and admit it, and to shape our national course so that it cannot happen.
As M. Briand said, peace is proclaimed; it remains necessary to organize it. Instead of spending so much of the time of this house in quarrelling about local matters of comparative unimportance, we should spend more time in discussing some of these larger world problems for the solution of which Canada cannot escape responsibility.

The only answer we could get from the Immigration department was, "Our ledger has no column for that item, and we are not responsible." We, being human could not see the men lie down and starve in the streets, so we had to put our hands in our pockets and help to keep these men for whom we had no responsibility and who had not come into the city by our asking. The mayor asked me to endeavour to have some provision made for repayment to the city of the expense incurred through these men having to be placed in the hospital.
I now come to the question of immigration itself. My friend the leader of the opposition

Supply-Ways and Means
said that Canada's pressing need is immigration. I entirely differ from him in that view.
I am glad to see that the United Farmers of Alberta and the labour people also differ with that proposition.

subtopic: DEBATE ON MOTION FOR ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That makes another
one.

subtopic: DEBATE ON MOTION FOR ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Canada herself should
decide who shall and who shall not come within her borders. It has been mooted that we hold this land in trust, that we have a certain responsibility to those people whose borders are crowded, and that if we do not open the doors some means will be found to force them. As a man whose adopted country is Canada, and as a man who has Canadian boys, I want to say that Canada is going to decide who shall and who shall not come within her borders.

subtopic: DEBATE ON MOTION FOR ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is time she did.

subtopic: DEBATE ON MOTION FOR ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Baldwin told Canada to go slowly, for there was plenty of time for immigration into this country of the proper sort. I am opposed to the spending of over two millions of dollars, as we did last year-

subtopic: DEBATE ON MOTION FOR ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Three millions.

subtopic: DEBATE ON MOTION FOR ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
-the spending of this amount to coax immigrants into Canada. The Leeds Mercury of England has the following to say on this subject:
But "spoon-fed" emigration by costly schemes on the grand scale is not the most likely to succeed. Assisted and stimulated emigration may be a good thing, but the best emigrant is the man who is convinced that he will have a better chance in another country and is willing to make an effort to get there.
Spending a couple of millions of dollars to induce people to come to Canada is not the way Canada will settle the distant parts of her territory. It is not the way the east was settled, neither is it the way the west was settled or should be settled. If we have immigrants coming to Canada they should come voluntarily, and they should be possessed of the proper information. The Department of Immigration has recently issued an atlas, which shows the settler under the most laudable, praiseworthy conditions. First, he has a little shack; by and by he has grown a little crop, then he has a larger crop, and finally there is a beautiful mansion.

subtopic: DEBATE ON MOTION FOR ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He never has the frost, by any chance?

subtopic: DEBATE ON MOTION FOR ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
But it omits to say that his crop may be destroyed by frost, or any of those things which go to make agriculture
undesirable. It is not a fair presentation of the case, and these immigrants coming to Canada should be given the other side of the picture. They should have the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.
There is another side of the question I would like to mention, and that is the character of the men that come into Canada. If a man is physically fit and has a considerable amount of muscle, and perhaps the amount of money required, we will allow him in. We had criminals in the city of Calgary this year who, when their history was traced, had committed the same crimes in the countries they had left to come to Canada. Then there was the case of the magistrate in the old country who told a criminal brought before him that if he would go to Canada he would not have to go to gaol. That is a deplorable state of affairs. Canada is not going to be made into another Botany Bay where criminals from England or elsewhere may be shipped in order to be rid of them.
I am opposed to the spending of so much money to coax people to come to Canada. The provinces should be consulted in these matters, but they seem to have no responsibility at all. The immigrants are left to shift for themselves, and they should be told of the hardships and difficulties as well as the pleasures. We want the class of men who will come on their own initiative and be willing to face the difficulties as well as to enjoy the successes.
Motion (Mr. Cayley) agreed to.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King, seconded by Mr. Robb, it was ordered that the address be engrossed and transmitted to His Excellency the Governor General by such members of the house as are of the honourable the Privy Council.
